topics.title: Design Snake & Ladder
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design Snake & Ladder: N players take turns rolling dice and move along a board of 100 cells; snakes send you down, ladders send you up, and the first to reach 100 wins. Interviewers use it to test a **game-engine abstraction**: clean entities, configurable rules and **Strategy** for dice and rule variations.

## Requirements

**Functional**
- Configurable board size, snakes and ladders (validated: no cycles, nothing starting at the end cell).
- 2+ players in a turn queue. One or more dice.
- Rule variants: exact roll needed to finish, extra turn on a 6, three 6s forfeits the turn.
- Report each move and the winner. Optionally continue to rank all players.

**Non-functional**
- Deterministic and testable: dice and randomness are injectable (seeded).
- Rule variants are configurable without changing the game loop.
- The board is validated once at setup, not during play.

## 1. Scope and chosen solution

I choose a 100-square board, six-sided dice, exact landing to win, one jump per landing and first winner ends the game. No bonus turn for six in this ruleset. The board validates jump endpoints and direction; snakes descend and ladders ascend.

## 2. Turn execution

```text
playTurn(playerId):
  verify active game and expected player
  roll injected dice, require 1..6
  candidate = position + roll
  if candidate > 100: final = old position
  else: final = jumpMap.getOrDefault(candidate,candidate)
  commit roll, old/final position and winner or next player
```

At 14 with roll 3 and ladder 17→38, final position is 38. At 97 with roll 5, it stays 97. One-jump resolution cannot loop even if arbitrary map data contains a cycle; I still reject invalid self-jumps and endpoints at construction. A chained-jump extension uses a visited set and rejects cycles. Concurrent turn calls serialize at Game, preventing two dice rolls for the same accepted turn/version. Expected dice value 3.5 does not equal net progress because jumps and overshoots alter movement.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![Design Snake & Ladder: Game uses Board; Game rotates Player; Game rolls through Dice; Game advances with TurnPolicy; Board resolves jumps JumpResolver; Game records MoveHistory](designs/lld-17.svg)](designs/lld-17.svg)

The **board** stores snakes and ladders, the **dice source** produces a roll, and the **game** owns turn order and player positions. Randomness is an input boundary, so tests should supply predetermined rolls rather than hope the right number appears.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![The game applies movement policy before resolving a jump.](lessons/lld-17-flow.svg)

*The game applies movement policy before resolving a jump.*

![Validate jump chains or restrict the board to one jump per landing.](lessons/lld-17-failure.svg)

*Validate jump chains or restrict the board to one jump per landing.*

### Selected algorithm

```java
// Rule sketch: exact landing; an overshoot leaves the position unchanged.
int advance(int current, int roll, int lastSquare) {
    if (roll < 1 || roll > 6) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
    int target = current + roll;
    return target > lastSquare ? current : target;
}
```

For a board with six-sided dice, the expected single roll is `(1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5`. That is not the expected net movement once snakes, ladders and overshoot rules apply. Avoid replacing the actual board process with this average when explaining game duration.

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Key abstractions

| Type | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `Game` | Turn loop, winner detection |
| `Board` | size, `Map<Integer, Integer> jumps` (start → end) |
| `Jump` (or `Snake`/`Ladder` subtypes) | start, end; a snake has end < start |
| `Player` | name, position |
| `Dice` (Strategy) | `StandardDice(count)`, `CrookedDice` (only even numbers), `FixedDice` for tests |
| `RuleSet` | `ExactFinishRule`, `ExtraTurnOnSix`, `ThreeSixesForfeit` |
| `BoardFactory` | Builds a board from config and validates it |

```java
int move(Player p, int roll) {
    int target = p.position() + roll;
    if (target > board.size()) return p.position();     // exact-finish rule
    return board.jumps().getOrDefault(target, target);   // O(1) snake/ladder
}
```

### Design decisions & trade-offs

**1. Snakes and ladders are the same thing.** Both are a jump from `start` to `end`. One `Map<Integer, Integer>` handles both in O(1). Separate classes add nothing except display labels. This is a nice "avoid needless inheritance" point.

**2. Dice as a Strategy.** It makes the game testable: inject `FixedDice(4, 2, 6)` to script a game. Variants (two dice, crooked dice) don't touch `Game`.

**3. Rules as composable objects.** Rule toggles change between house variants. A list of `Rule` objects consulted in order (`afterRoll`, `canFinish`, `grantsExtraTurn`) keeps the turn loop stable.

**4. Turn order.** Use a `Deque<Player>`: poll, play, offer back (unless they finished or forfeit). With an extra-turn rule, re-offer to the front.

**5. Board validation.** Reject jumps that start at 1 or 100, jumps that land on another jump's start (chains), and two jumps from the same cell. Fail at construction, not mid-game.

### Ownership, boundaries and invariants

**Central design question:** Make game rules explicit, especially overshoot and whether special squares chain.

Board maps starting squares to Jump targets; Game owns Players and current turn. Dice is an injected source of bounded values. MovePolicy handles exact-finish rules; TurnPolicy handles extra turns. Randomness is a dependency so tests can be deterministic.

**Correctness rule:** Player positions stay within board bounds, every jump target is valid, and terminal games stop accepting moves. A malformed jump cycle cannot cause an infinite turn.

```text
game(id,board_size,current_player,version); player(id,position); jump(from_square,to_square); turn(id,roll,result)
```

### End-to-end execution trace

Verify current player; obtain a dice value from the configured dice; compute tentative square; apply overshoot policy; resolve the allowed snake/ladder behavior with a visited set if chaining is supported; commit the final position; declare victory or advance turn.

### Concurrency and recovery walkthrough

Two roll commands for the same turn use different random values. A turn request ID and aggregate version prevent both from advancing the game; persist the chosen roll before returning success.

### Policy choices and extension seams

A map from square to destination is sufficient for snakes and ladders. Subclasses for every snake add little value. Strategy becomes useful for house rules, number of dice or finish behavior.

### Edge cases that change the design

Reject jumps from or to invalid squares, duplicate jump origins and forbidden start/end cells. Decide whether landing on a ladder leads to another jump. Do not quietly hard-code a popular house rule as the only valid ruleset.

**Topic-specific cases:** Deterministic dice; overshoot; exact finish; cycle detection; extra-turn rule; duplicate roll command; board configuration validation.

### Further reading

- [Java 21 concurrency contracts](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/package-summary.html) — synchronization and executor semantics.
- [PostgreSQL transaction isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html) — database guarantees differ from process locks.

### Work through extension seams

Represent jumps as data `start -> end`; validate endpoints inside the board and forbid a zero-length jump. If the chosen rules allow at most one jump per turn, document that instead of accidentally chaining jumps because the implementation uses recursion.

Rules such as “roll six again” and “three sixes lose the turn” belong in a turn policy with an explicit roll history. They do not belong in the physical dice implementation. A replay log should store actual rolls and committed moves so results remain reproducible even if a random generator changes.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**How do you test a ladder landing?** Inject a roll that reaches its starting square and assert the final destination.

**Should a winner keep receiving turns?** No. Define whether the game ends at first victory or ranks all players, then enforce that terminal policy.

## 7. Closing answer

I make board jumps data and inject dice results, while Game owns deterministic turn transitions. Exact-landing and one-jump-per-landing are explicit policies. A move log records actual rolls, so tests and replay do not depend on randomness.

topics.title: Metrics / Time-Series System
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Design a metrics / time-series monitoring system (like Prometheus at scale, Datadog metrics or M3): collect numeric measurements (CPU, request rate, latency percentiles) from many services, store them efficiently, power dashboards and alerts, and keep long-term history cheaply. The specialist topics are **time-series storage**, **compression**, **aggregation**, **retention and downsampling**, and **cardinality**.

## Requirements

**Functional**
- Ingest `(metric name, labels, timestamp, value)` samples every 10–60 s.
- Query ranges with aggregation (`sum by (service) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))`), percentiles, dashboards.
- Alert rules evaluated every ~30 s. Retention: raw 15 days, 1-minute rollups for a year.

**Non-functional**
- Write-heavy and append-only. Dashboards return in < 1 s for common queries.

**Scale:** 10M active series × 1 sample/10 s = **1M samples/s**. At ~1.5 bytes per sample after compression, that's ~130 GB/day.

## 1. Scope and selected semantics

I ingest counters, gauges and histograms, query recent/history windows and evaluate alerts. I choose tenant-scoped label validation, append-oriented time blocks and rollups. Unbounded request/user identifiers are excluded from metric labels; logs/traces serve that lookup need.

## 2. Data and query contract

```text
Series identity = tenant + metricName + canonical label set
Sample = seriesId,timestamp,value; histogram = compatible bucket counts
Query: rate(request_total[5m]), histogram quantile over summed bucket rates
Alert: expression,window,holdDuration,missingDataPolicy
```

Ingest validates units, timestamp range, duplicates and cardinality limits before append. Blocks are compacted and queried by time/series indexes. Counters are converted to rates with reset handling. Histograms merge counts only with compatible definitions; averaging p99 values is invalid. For 200 services×20 routes×5 statuses×3 regions, 60,000 series at 15-second sampling produce 4,000 samples/s before instances/buckets. Adding arbitrary user IDs destroys that bound. Alerts separately represent false, true and missing/unknown data; absent samples are not automatically healthy zeros.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![Metrics / Time-Series System: Instrumented services samples Collectors; Collectors tenant validation Ingest and limits; Ingest and limits append series Time-series blocks; Query engine range reads Time-series blocks; Alert evaluator evaluates windows Query engine; Time-series blocks downsamples Long-term rollups](designs/hld-17.svg)](designs/hld-17.svg)

A **counter** increases over time, a **gauge** represents a current value, and a **histogram** summarizes a distribution. A **series** is one metric plus one specific label set. User IDs as labels can create millions of series.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![Collection, aggregation and evaluation have separate timing semantics.](lessons/hld-17-flow.svg)

*Collection, aggregation and evaluation have separate timing semantics.*

![Bound label choices before accepting arbitrary per-request values.](lessons/hld-17-failure.svg)

*Bound label choices before accepting arbitrary per-request values.*

### Calculate series count

For 200 services × 20 routes × 5 status classes × 3 regions, there are 60,000 combinations before instance labels and histogram buckets. Adding one million user IDs can multiply this beyond a usable design. At 60,000 series sampled every 15 seconds, samples arrive at 4,000/s; histogram bucket series increase this further.

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Architecture

- **Collection:** pull (Prometheus scrapes `/metrics`) or push (agents, StatsD/OTel). A push gateway is used for short-lived jobs.
- **Ingest:** a distributor hashes the series ID (name + sorted labels) to ingester shards (consistent hashing, replication factor 3). Ingesters keep recent data in memory with a **write-ahead log** and periodically flush immutable **blocks** (2 h) to object storage.
- **Storage format:** per series, timestamps delta-of-delta encoded and values XOR-compressed (Facebook **Gorilla**), giving ~1.3 bytes/sample. An inverted index from label to series IDs answers selectors.
- **Compaction and downsampling:** background jobs merge blocks and create 5-minute and 1-hour rollups (min, max, sum, count, so averages stay correct).
- **Query layer:** fans out to ingesters (recent) and the store (historical), merges, and caches results by time-aligned step.

### Key design decisions & trade-offs

**1. Pull vs. push.** Pull gives easy health detection ("target down") and central control, but needs service discovery and struggles across firewalls and with short jobs. Push suits ephemeral and edge workloads, but you must protect against floods.

**2. Cardinality is the real scaling limit.** Labels like `userId` or `requestId` create millions of series and blow memory and the index. Enforce label limits per metric and reject or aggregate high-cardinality labels at ingest.

**3. Percentiles.** You can't average p99s across hosts. Store **histograms** (fixed buckets, or sketches like DDSketch or t-digest) and compute quantiles at query time from merged buckets.

**4. Downsampling trade-off.** Rollups make year-long queries cheap but lose spikes. Keep min and max alongside avg so peaks remain visible.

**5. Why not a general SQL DB?** Generic B-trees and row storage waste space and write throughput. A TSDB's append-only, time-partitioned, columnar, compressed design is 10–50× more efficient.

### Scope, guarantees and sizing assumptions

**Correctness requirement:** Metric identity includes labels and type; aggregation respects counter resets and time semantics.

Assume 100,000 targets x 200 series sampled every 15 seconds: 20 million active series and about 1.33 million samples/s. At an illustrative 16 raw bytes/sample: about 21.3 MB/s before compression and indexes.

### API contracts and data ownership

```text
Scrape/export endpoint or remote-write batch; range query with step; alert-rule definition
```

```text
Logical records (outline, not complete DDL):
series(id,tenant,name,labels,type); sample(series_id,timestamp,value); rule(id,expression,window,for_duration)

Primary access/partitioning boundary:
metric_name + sorted label set + tenant; time for partition lifecycle
```

### Build the architecture in stages

**Stage 3 — Partition and isolate.** Partition around metric_name + sorted label set + tenant; time for partition lifecycle. Track ownership with a routing epoch or a database-native partition mechanism. Move virtual buckets or copy/backfill data with a verified cutover, rather than changing a modulo divisor and assuming records move themselves. Isolate bulk/background workloads from the latency-sensitive path and test the busiest tenant independently.

### Trace the critical request

Collect samples; validate timestamps and label cardinality; shard by series; append to time blocks; compact and downsample; query retrieves blocks and merges by label semantics; evaluate alert rules with explicit missing-data policy.

### Deep dive: the decision that changes this system

A user_id label can turn one metric into millions of series. Counters are monotonic between resets; computing rates needs reset handling. Summing averages without weights is wrong. Histograms can aggregate bucket counts under compatible boundaries; precomputed quantiles generally cannot be averaged into a global p99.

### Failure and race-condition walkthrough

A scrape gap is not necessarily zero. Duplicate or reordered samples need store-specific acceptance rules. Alert evaluation during missing data should distinguish unavailable telemetry from healthy zero error rate.

### Security, tenancy and lifecycle

### Trade-offs and a starting recommendation

Pull simplifies service discovery and health visibility; push suits short-lived jobs and disconnected agents. Downsampling reduces cost but discards granularity; keep retention tiers aligned with debugging needs.

Series cardinality, ingest lag, query p99, dropped samples, alert evaluation delay and storage amplification.

**Test matrix:** Counter reset, missing scrape, high-cardinality label attack, histogram aggregation, out-of-order sample, query spanning compaction and alert flapping.

### Follow-up questions with answers

**What cannot be eventually consistent here?** The operation establishing this guarantee: Metric identity includes labels and type; aggregation respects counter resets and time semantics.

**What is the first scaling pressure to test?** Use the actual workload: Assume 100,000 targets x 200 series sampled every 15 seconds: 20 million active series and about 1.33 million samples/s. At an illustrative 16 raw bytes/sample: about 21.3 MB/s before compression and indexes.

**Which failure would invalidate the naive design?** A scrape gap is not necessarily zero. Duplicate or reordered samples need store-specific acceptance rules. Alert evaluation during missing data should distinguish unavailable telemetry from healthy zero error rate.

**Why not introduce every distributed component immediately?** Pull simplifies service discovery and health visibility; push suits short-lived jobs and disconnected agents. Downsampling reduces cost but discards granularity; keep retention tiers aligned with debugging needs.

**How would you demonstrate the design works?** Counter reset, missing scrape, high-cardinality label attack, histogram aggregation, out-of-order sample, query spanning compaction and alert flapping. Keep the expected invariant and recovery outcome visible in the results.

### Further reading

- [PostgreSQL isolation and anomalies](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html).
- [Apache Kafka delivery and transaction design](https://kafka.apache.org/41/design/design/).
- [Redis rate-limiter design](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use-cases/rate-limiter/) for atomic shared-state examples.

### Work through semantics

Counters can reset when a process restarts, so rate calculations must account for resets. Averaging two p99 values does not yield the combined p99. Aggregate compatible histogram bucket counts, then estimate the percentile. Preserve units and bucket boundaries across deployments.

Downsampling reduces long-term storage but loses detail. An hourly average cannot recover a ten-second outage. Alerts need a policy for missing samples; treating missing as zero can falsely report healthy traffic or trigger nonsense ratios. Keep alert evaluation lag and ingestion lag observable.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Is a user ID a good metric label?** Usually not for unbounded populations; use logs/traces or another bounded aggregation.

**Can a gauge be safely summed across replicas?** Only when its meaning is additive; temperature is not equivalent to active-request count.

## 7. Closing answer

Metric meaning and bounded cardinality are the core contract. I store labeled timestamped series, aggregate compatible histogram buckets before estimating percentiles, and handle counter resets/missing data explicitly. Retention and downsampling trade detail for cost rather than promising recovery of discarded detail.

topics.title: AI Observability & Evaluation
topics.concepts: Tracing, metrics, token usage, evaluation, hallucination detection
topics.markdown:
## Problem

Explain how to observe and evaluate LLM applications in production: tracing every model, tool and retrieval call; tracking tokens, latency, cost and errors; building offline evaluation suites and online quality monitoring; and detecting hallucinations and regressions. Show how Spring AI's Micrometer-based observability and evaluators fit in.

## Requirements

- What to trace: prompts (redacted), model and parameters, retrieved docs, tool calls, tokens, latency, finish reasons.
- Metrics and dashboards: cost per request or feature, p95 latency, error and refusal rates.
- Offline evals: golden datasets, metrics (exact match, faithfulness, relevance), LLM-as-judge.
- Online signals: user feedback, guardrail triggers, drift.
- Hallucination detection and groundedness checks for RAG.

## 1. Selected evaluation system

I evaluate retrieval, supported answers, abstention, permissions and operating cost on fixed case revisions. Deterministic stubs test infrastructure failures; live-model cases measure language behaviour. A 200 response is not an answer-quality success.

## 2. Case and trace schemas

```text
EvalCase: input,authorizedCorpusRevision,expectedSources,answerability,rubric
Run: prompt/model/index versions,caseId,actualOutcome,scoringVersion
Trace: source IDs,tool calls,retries,token usage,durations,terminationReason
Release gate: per-slice thresholds AND zero defined critical violations
```

If 90 of 100 answerable cases succeed but all 20 absent-answer cases fabricate, I report both populations instead of “90% accuracy.” One cross-tenant disclosure fails the critical isolation gate even if overall average improves. Citation validity and actual claim support are separate scores.

For each change I compare the same inputs and inspect regressions. An LLM judge uses a versioned rubric and human-labelled calibration cases; verbosity preference or shared model blind spots can bias it. Logs retain necessary versions/IDs without copying unrestricted private text. First-token, completion, tool/retrieval and queue times identify different latency causes. Small sample counts are published so apparent precision does not conceal uncertainty.

## 3. Final design diagram

[![AI Observability & Evaluation: Versioned cases frozen inputs Evaluation runner; Evaluation runner exercises System under test; System under test versions usage Execution traces; Execution traces support and latency Scoring rubrics; Human calibration calibrates Scoring rubrics; Scoring rubrics sliced criteria Release gate](designs/ai-17.svg)](designs/ai-17.svg)

A **trace** connects retrieval, model and tool steps. A **dataset case** specifies input, context and expected evidence/behaviour. A **metric slice** groups results by a meaningful condition such as language or answerability. An **LLM judge** is another imperfect model, not an unquestionable oracle.

## 4. Critical operation: worked execution

![Versioned inputs and scoring rules make comparisons meaningful.](lessons/ai-17-flow.svg)

*Versioned inputs and scoring rules make comparisons meaningful.*

![Security and rare high-impact cases need separate gates.](lessons/ai-17-failure.svg)

*Security and rare high-impact cases need separate gates.*

### Calculate the right denominator

If 90 of 100 answerable cases succeed but all 20 unanswerable cases get fabricated answers, reporting “90% accuracy” omits a major failure class. Report answerable success, correct abstention, unsupported claims and forbidden disclosures separately. A small test suite gives uncertain estimates; label its size and avoid precision the sample cannot support.

## 5. Detailed decisions, algorithms and failure behaviour

### Mechanism and rationale

**Design question:** How do you know a model or prompt change improved the product rather than one demonstration?

Evaluation separates retrieval, generation, tool use and end-to-end business outcomes. A golden set contains input, authorized evidence, expected properties and failure cases. Model-judged scores are useful noisy signals that need calibration against humans and deterministic checks.

### Architecture and contracts

```text
Version dataset -> run candidate/baseline -> collect traces -> deterministic checks -> calibrated rubric scoring -> slice analysis -> release gate -> online monitoring

Application contracts (design outline):
EvalCase(id,input,expectedEvidence,checks,slice); EvalResult(pass,reason,usage,latency,traceId)
```

Collect Micrometer/OpenTelemetry-compatible counts and duration traces with prompt/model/index versions. Keep raw text opt-in and redacted; use a stub model for deterministic infrastructure tests.

### Worked reasoning and capacity example

If 90 of 100 questions pass, report 90/100 with dataset scope and uncertainty; a 1-point change on that sample is not strong evidence of universal improvement. Separate cost and latency distributions instead of averaging them into a single opaque score.

### Java and Spring AI implementation outline

```java
record EvalCase(String id, String input, java.util.Set<String> expectedEvidence) {}
record EvalResult(boolean authorized, boolean supported, long latencyMillis) {}
// Aggregate by dataset slice; keep per-case failures and baseline results.
```

### Design decisions and alternatives

Use exact checks for schemas, authorization and amounts; rubrics for relevance and support; human review for ambiguous high-impact cases. Never put test examples into the prompt’s few-shot training context.

### Failure scenario and safe recovery

A model judge prefers fluent fabricated answers to short grounded ones. Include adversarial unsupported answers during calibration and require evidence-level checks. A green aggregate can hide a badly regressed minority language.

### Security, privacy and provenance

A benchmark without versioned inputs and scoring rules cannot be reproduced. Do not claim production reliability from a handful of handpicked examples.


**Verification criteria:** Track supported answer rate, retrieval recall, task completion, unsafe action rate, cost and latency by slice; use deterministic pass/fail gates for critical invariants.

### Further reading

- [Spring AI 1.1 ChatClient and request APIs](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/chatclient.html).
- [Spring AI tool-execution boundary](https://docs.spring.io/spring-ai/reference/1.1/api/tools.html).
- [MCP specification, versioned protocol concepts](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18).
- [Original RAG research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) and [Transformer research](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) for background rather than framework instructions.

### Work through useful traces

Record prompt/model/index versions, source IDs, token usage, duration, tool names, retries and termination reason. Raw private text should not be the default telemetry payload. An incident needs enough provenance to reproduce the pipeline without turning logs into a second unrestricted document store.

Use deterministic stubs for deadline, retry, authorization and schema tests. Use model evaluations for language behaviour, with rubric and human calibration where appropriate. A judge may prefer verbose answers or share the tested model's blind spots; combine automated signals with inspected examples.

## 6. Interviewer follow-ups

**Is provider latency equal to user-perceived latency?** No. Retrieval, queues, tools and post-validation also contribute.

**Does a high citation count prove grounding?** No. Check claim support, not decorative references.

## 7. Closing answer

I measure task quality and operational execution separately, version the test conditions and gate critical failures independently of averages. Traces explain which pipeline stage failed, while human-calibrated rubrics prevent an unreviewed model judge from becoming the sole authority.
